html:
The Ute are a people of the mountains and high plateaus of today's Colorado and Utah, with lands reaching into New Mexico and Wyoming. Their language is a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family. The state of Utah is named after them.

They lived in a dozen or so bands, moving between mountain hunting grounds in summer and sheltered valleys in winter, hunting deer, elk and bison and gathering seeds and roots.

The Ute were among the first peoples of the north to get horses from the Spanish of New Mexico in the 1600s, and they became mounted traders and raiders. They traded and fought with the Pueblos and the Navajo, and for a time were allied with the Comanche.

Miners poured into the Colorado mountains from 1859. After the Meeker incident of 1879, when White River Ute killed an Indian agent and soldiers, the United States forced most Ute out of Colorado into Utah. Three Ute tribes survive today: the Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute in Colorado and the Northern Ute in Utah. See also Ute and horses on the Plains.
